lead: Skin cycling is a skincare routine that rotates evenings of active ingredients with evenings of recovery so that exfoliants and retinoids can be used for clearer, smoother, more even skin with less irritation. It is credited to New York dermatologist Whitney Bowe, whose framing was aimed at patients who were overdoing actives, and it spread widely on TikTok in 2022.[1][3]

The standard four-night cycle uses a chemical exfoliant on night one, a retinoid on night two, and no actives on nights three and four, when moisturising and barrier-supporting products are used instead. Mornings are the same each day: gentle cleansing and broad-spectrum sunscreen.[1][3] Proponents say the approach delivers the benefits of strong actives, such as smoother texture and more radiance, while giving the skin barrier time to recover.[1][3]

No published clinical trial has tested this specific schedule. Coverage of the trend notes that its support comes from the evidence for each ingredient class and from the dermatological view that rest reduces irritation.[3] Accounts differ on the exact start date, with Grokipedia dating the introduction to April 2021 and magazine coverage to 2022.[1][3]

chain: Alternate exfoliant and retinoid nights with rest nights
Skin tolerates actives with less dryness and redness
angle.text: Skin cycling is a schedule for using exfoliating acids and retinoids, the actives people use for texture, tone and breakouts, in a way that is easier on the skin barrier. People use it to keep up with these actives without the irritation that makes them stop.

paras: Night one uses a chemical exfoliant such as an alpha, beta or poly hydroxy acid. Night two uses a retinoid, either over-the-counter retinol or prescription tretinoin, applied to freshly exfoliated skin. Nights three and four contain no actives and focus on hydration and barrier repair with ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides and niacinamide.[1][3][4]

The daytime routine is constant: gentle cleansing, optional moisturiser and broad-spectrum sunscreen, because exfoliants and retinoids increase sun sensitivity.[1] A dermatology practice describing the method suggests moisturising before a retinoid, especially around the eyes and nose creases, to reduce irritation.[4]

Variants exist with more recovery nights for sensitive skin and, for experienced users, fewer; some versions use a five-night cycle with an extra recovery night between exfoliation and retinoid.[1][3][4]

Bowe is credited with coining the term. One magazine account quotes her framing as a framework for patients overdoing actives and says it spread across social platforms in 2022, becoming one of the most-searched skincare routines the following year.[3] Grokipedia dates the introduction to April 2021.[1]

Dermatologists describe the approach as consistent with the long-standing practice of pairing potent actives with rest. Coverage notes that people already using a single active without irritation may not need it, and that retinoids are not used in pregnancy, which is a question for a clinician.[3] General references describe over-exfoliation as able to irritate skin and damage its barrier.[2]

A dermatology practice presenting the method describes it as adaptable to different skin types and recommends a consultation to tailor it.[4] Noted limitations include the time visible change can take and that it does not replace professional treatment for conditions such as cystic acne or melasma.[1]

timeline.event: Grokipedia dates Whitney Bowe's introduction of skin cycling to April.[1]
The routine spreads widely through social media, especially TikTok.[1][3]
Skin cycling is among the most-searched skincare routines, per magazine coverage citing Google search data.[3]

lore.intro: Skin cycling is discussed in skincare and looksmaxxing communities as a way to use retinoids and acids without a damaged skin barrier.[1][3]

claims.claim: Alternating actives with rest nights gives retinoid results with less irritation
claims.believers: Proponents say recovery nights reduce dryness and redness and help users build tolerance to retinoids and exfoliants.[1][3]
claims.experts: Dermatologists describe it as a reasonable framework, but no study has tested the schedule itself; support comes from the evidence for each ingredient class.[3]

claims.claim: Skin cycling suits sensitive, acne-prone or barrier-damaged skin
claims.believers: Its proponents describe it as suitable for many skin types, with extra recovery nights as needed.[1][4]
claims.experts: It is not described as a substitute for professional treatment of severe acne, and general references caution that over-exfoliation can harm the skin barrier.[2][4]

name: Skin cycling

card.summary: A four-night rotation of acid, retinoid and two rest nights; popular and plausible, but the schedule itself has never been trialled.
card.note: Retinoids and exfoliants increase sun sensitivity; daily sunscreen is part of the method.

quick.overview:
Skin cycling rotates a four-night routine: an exfoliating acid, then a retinoid, then two nights with no actives. It was introduced by dermatologist Whitney Bowe in 2021 and went viral on TikTok.

Supporters say it cuts irritation while still using strong ingredients. No clinical study has tested the schedule itself.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that rest nights let the skin barrier recover between exfoliation and retinoid use, so irritation builds less than with daily actives.
quick.risks: Exfoliants and retinoids can cause dryness, redness and sun sensitivity, so sunscreen is part of the routine. It is not described as a replacement for professional treatment of severe acne.
